## Statement

No study has crossed bridge type, prior specification, target-population definition and outcome model in a factorial design scored on decision reversals, so there is no ranking of which structural choice most often flips a recommendation. Individual factors have been examined: Jiang et al. 2025 (10.1017/rsm.2025.10) construct a MAIC paradox in which switching which trial supplies IPD reverses which drug is judged superior, and Cassidy et al. 2023 (10.1016/j.jval.2023.07.001) show across 80 comparisons that MAICs shift estimates toward the treatment whose IPD is held. The four choices are also not equivalent in kind: changing the target population changes the estimand and changing the bridge changes the identifying assumptions, whereas a prior changes regularization and the posterior and an outcome-model specification usually changes the estimator, not the estimand.

## Why it is open

The four choices are made at different points in the workflow by different people, so no single analysis varies them jointly and their interactions are never observed. Conventional sensitivity analysis varies a parameter inside a fixed structure and so does not reach choices that change the identifying assumptions or the target population. The factorial study is feasible with ordinary scenario or simulation methods, so what is missing is that nobody has run it, not a missing identification principle; the design must hold a common decision target and use only coherent combinations, because a reversal between two target populations can mean two different decision questions rather than sensitivity of one.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Jiang et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1017/rsm.2025.10) | Shows that the target-population choice alone can reverse which treatment is judged superior in MAIC, quantifying one of the four factors. |
| [Cassidy et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2023.07.001) | Compares 80 MAIC estimates with the corresponding standard anchored ITCs across 17 publications and finds MAICs systematically favor the IPD holder's treatment. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Run the factorial simulation with a common decision target held fixed and only coherent factor combinations crossed, reporting the frequency and direction of decision reversals attributable to each factor and to their interactions. Separate factors that redefine the estimand, meaning target population and bridge, from those that change identification or estimation, meaning prior and outcome model, and report them on that footing rather than as one undifferentiated sensitivity. Use the resulting ranking to decide which structural choices must be prespecified in a protocol.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. No study has jointly varied bridge type, prior specification, target-population definition and outcome model in a factorial design scored on decision reversals, so there is no ranking of which structural choice most often flips a recommendation. Individual factors have been examined: target-population choice has been shown to reverse MAIC conclusions, and estimator choice (MAIC vs standard anchored ITC) has been shown empirically to shift estimates in a consistent direction.

**The source titled this.** "Decision sensitivity to bridge, prior, target and model unmeasured" The title says this sensitivity is unmeasured, but the audit found target-population choice and estimator choice each already shown to change conclusions.

**The source said.** "How sensitive a reimbursement decision is to the analyst's choice of bridge, prior, target population and outcome model has never been quantified. There is therefore no evidence about which structural modeling choice most often flips a recommendation, and no basis for ranking which choices must be pre-specified."

**What was wrong with it.** The source said this sensitivity has never been quantified and that all four choices change the estimand. The literature auditor found two of the four already quantified (Jiang et al. 2025 for target population, Cassidy et al. 2023 for estimator choice), and GPT-5.6 Sol found the estimand claim false for prior and outcome-model specification, which change estimation rather than the estimand.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **open / overstated.** No factorial study crossing bridge type, prior, target population and outcome model and scoring decision reversals exists, so the proposed direction is genuinely unoccupied. But 'has never been quantified' is too strong for one of the four factors. Jiang et al. 2025 (Res Synth Methods, doi 10.1017/rsm.2025.10, full text read) constructs an explicit 'MAIC paradox' in which the comparative-effectiveness conclusion reverses purely by switching which trial supplies IPD, i.e. by changing the target population, and notes NICE DSU TSD 18 already documented a real secukinumab/adalimumab case where two MAICs reached opposing conclusions. Cassidy et al. 2023 (doi 10.1016/j.jval.2023.07.001) empirically compared 80 MAIC estimates against the corresponding standard anchored ITCs and found MAICs systematically favor the IPD-holder's treatment, quantifying the estimator-choice factor. Phillippo et al. 2018 threshold analysis quantifies how far evidence must move before the recommendation flips, though for data perturbations rather than structural choices. So target population and estimator choice have each been shown to flip or shift conclusions; what is missing is the joint factorial evaluation and the prior and outcome-model arms.
    Cites 10.1017/rsm.2025.10: Demonstrates that the target-population choice alone can reverse which treatment is judged superior, partially quantifying one of the four factors..
    Cites 10.1016/j.jval.2023.07.001: Empirically quantifies the estimator-choice factor across 80 comparisons from 17 publications..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **not-a-problem / overstated.** The proposed sensitivity exercise is feasible using ordinary scenario, posterior-predictive, or factorial simulation, so no new statistical identification principle is missing. More importantly, C3 is false as a blanket statement. Changing the target population changes the estimand; changing a bridge usually changes the identifying assumptions or information path; changing a prior changes regularization and the posterior, not the estimand; and changing an outcome-model specification ordinarily changes the estimator or model, not the estimand, unless the outcome, horizon, or effect measure also changes. Factors cannot always be crossed independently because some combinations are incoherent. A decision reversal between different target populations may reflect a different decision question rather than sensitivity of one estimand. The claim that this has never been quantified is an uncited literature claim outside the technical evidence supplied.

Decision path
:   `R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)`

:::
